newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: NEW S.AFRICA OIL FIELDS REQUIRE TAX REFORM - SOEKOR.
newsitem.headline: NEW S.AFRICA OIL FIELDS REQUIRE TAX REFORM - SOEKOR.

text.p: South African state-owned exploration company Soekor, gearing up tap the country's first offshore oil field next February, said on Thursday that tax reforms were needed to encourage further upstream development.
Chief executive Joggie Heuser said Soekor had petitioned the government to introduce a fixed 30 to 35 percent tax on upstream oil and gas companies.
Addressing the Africa Upstream conference, Heuser said it was "totally unacceptable" that oil and gas companies faced an effective 71 percent tax rate.
"This is enough to chase away potential foreign investors," Heuser said.

He said he had also asked for a stand-alone Oil and Gas Act to provide investors with regulatory certainty. The laws covering the upstream oil and gas industry were currently tangled with those covering other minerals, he noted.
Heuser said he had submitted these and other suggestions about how to attract foreign investment to the government which appeared to be "seriously considering" them.
Soekor's research had identified potential oil and gas reserves in eight offshore geological basins, but only one was being exploited at present.
This was the Bredasdorp Basin, in which oil-from-gas producer Mossgas was tapping the F-A field.
However, Soekor and its 20-percent partner Energy Africa are due to start oil production in the E-BT oil field, now called the Oribi oil field, in February 1997.

The Oribi field will be South Africa's first offshore oil field. It is expected to produce at 20,000 to 25,000 barrels per day, enough to meet around six percent of South Africa's crude oil requirements.
The low-sulphur oil, comparable in quality to Brent, could go to refineries in either Cape Town or Durban, although Soekor has not negotiated any fixed contracts, a company spokesman said.

"The task now is to start attracting international investment and participation in our search (for new reserves), in competition with other counties whose prospectivity is higher and offer less risks," Heuser said.
Soekor has held several licensing rounds but had failed to attract investors because offshore fields are regarded as gas prone and government investment incentives inadequate, he said.
Heuser said that although South Africa's offshore basins tended to be gas prone, he believed that recent technological advances, especially in deep water exploration, made more oil finds possible.
